newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 27.

text.p: THE DOMINION

Rescuers battled strong winds in the Cook Strait to save five people on Tuesday, including a paraplegic and his young son, after their boat was swamped a kilometre out from Wellington's Owhiro Bay. Page 1.

The insurance and savings industry called on politicians on Tuesday to stop debating superannuation behind closed doors. Investment Savings and Insurance Association chief executive Roger Gill called for the issue to be urgently debated in public. "This is an issue fundamental to the security and
welfare of all New Zealanders," Gill said. "It is a highly complex area and too important to be the subject of political tradeoffs without input from all relevant interest groups." Page 1.

National has been making soundings with ACT NZ about bringing it into a coalition with a National-NZ First government, ACT and National sources said on Tuesday. ACT's caucus is due to meet Deputy Prime Minister Don McKinnon on Wednesday afternoon to discuss the relationship between ACT and National, after a meeting between Prime Minister Jim Bolger and
ACT leader Richard Prebble last week. Page 2.

NZ First leader Winston Peters denied on Tuesday that his party's compulsory retirement savings policy had changed, while his press secretary accepted there were differences and struggled to explain them. Page 2.

NZ First leader Winston Peters has predicted that the coalition soon to be struck is likely to last beyond the next election. Peters said the coalition's performance would be tested by the public, and if the response was positive it would
probably continue beyond the 1999 election. However, he said NZ First would not campaign at the next election with its coalition partner. Page 2.

New Zealand's biggest pulp and paper maker, Carter Holt Harvey, will soon announce detailed plans to modernise the Kinleith pulp and paper mill in the central North Island at an expected cost of up to $300 million. Carter Holt said on Tuesday that details of the "major development" would be revealed at a ceremony at Kinleith on December 5. Carter Holt shares rose five cents to $3.23 on Tuesday. The Government could have made a mistake by ruling the Baumol-Willig pricing rule off-limits, Commerce Commission chairman Alan Bollard says. The pricing rule allows a firm to charge lost monopoly profits to a competitor needing access to its services. Page 18.

Telecom rival Clear called on the government on Tuesday to set January 1 as a deadline for the first stage of number portability. This week the Telecommunications Users Association also called for the government to act on the issue. Number portability, allowing customers to keep their phone numbers if they shift providers, is considered crucial by Clear to entering the local telephone market. Telecom spokesman Clive Litt
ASB Bank has reported a 24 percent increase in after-tax profit to $18.2 million for the three months to September 30, but it does not expect to maintain that level of growth. Page 18.

Any benefits from the high dollar that could be passed on by producers were being negated by increasing costs, the Exporters Institute said on Tuesday in response to the producer price index figures. Input prices of goods and services increased on average 0.2 percent in the September quarter and output prices rose more quickly, at 0.4 percent, according to Statistics New
Zealand. Page 19.

Sembawang Corporation, a member of the Asian consortium that owns 20 percent of Brierley Investments, said it was merging its ship repair and marine engineering businesses with Jurong Shipyard, triggering a general takeover offer for Jurong. Page 19.
Life insurance and superannuation companies bounced back strongly in the June year, with profits up by 240 percent, according to Life Office Association figures out on Tuesday night. Page 27.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

New Zealanders are being hospitalised with critical dental problems because they fear -- or cannot afford visits to -- the dentist. In one case this year, a man spent three months in intensive care units at Middlemore and Greenlane hospitals in Auckland -- at a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars --
after pus spread through his jaw, neck, chest and endangered his heart.

Labour and Alliance leaders will hold a crucial meeting at Parliament on Wednesday afternoon, the first in the formal stages of firming up Alliance support for a Labour-NZ First coalition. NZ First leader Winston Peters has left Labour with the task of delivering Alliance support. While they met, National's caucus will be updated on its talks with NZ First, including its demand for six cabinet posts out of 15. Accepting that would force Prime Minister Jim Bolger to dump at least
seven ministers.

As the coalition negotiations enter the last lap, the financial markets are becoming nervous at what National may give away for a deal. The nervousness emerged on Tuesday in a commentary by Bankers' Trust chief economist David Plank entitled: "A National-New Zealand First Coalition: Good at Any Price? We Don't Think So." In it, he expresses concern at media reports that National may offer major policy concessions to stay in office, saying if that were to happen, it could be detrimental to the longer-term health of the economy.

The Waitakere, North Shore and Rodney councils are looking to cash in on their entitlement to Power New Zealand shares. They have retained Bankers' Trust to negotiate with potential buyers, with Mercury Energy and Utilicorp the obvious candidates. What the councils have right now that they can sell is unclear: they do not possess the shares, or control the right to vote them, or receive any dividends from them. Collectively, the councils stand to receive 10.7 percent of Power New Zealand, but not until 2004.

Kiwi Gold is investigating opportunities to enter the pearling industry. A director Harley Whitcombe said on Tuesday a pearling operation in Western Australia was being looked at, as well as opportunities in Vietnam, and the Middle East.

The strength of the New Zealand dollar against its United States counterpart over the past two years has cost the seafood industry $200 million in exports, according to Sanford managing director David Anderson.

Clear Communications on Tuesday called for government action to secure telephone number portability, saying the lack of it remained one of the major impediments to competition in the local market. Recent research it had commissioned found 45 percent of business consumers said they were quite likely or very likely to switch phone companies, even with no price differential, if they could keep the same number, Clear chief executive Andrew Makin said.
South Eastern Utilities said on Tuesday that a full year of cost savings from just-negotiated transmission charges and efficiency gains could boost its annual after-tax profit by $1.5 million.
